newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Serbian opposition propose "deadline" for Milosevic.
newsitem.headline: Serbian opposition propose "deadline" for Milosevic.

text.p: Serbian opposition leaders, rallying crowds on the 60th day of protests across Serbia, said on Thursday there should be a deadline for the government to meet their demands to reinstate annulled elections.

"I propose that we issue them a deadline for fully recognising the election results, and to say that after that deadline not a single institution in Serbia will have any legitimacy," Vesna Pesic, a co-leader of the Zajedno (Together) coalition, told demonstrators in Belgrade.
"After that deadline we will get all of Serbia on its feet -- we have no reason to waste any more time," Pesic told a crowd of about 10,000 to 15,000 in Republic Square.

Vuk Draskovic, another Zajedno leader, said the time for the government to restore the results of the annulled November 17 polls, in which the opposition swept 14 of Serbia's 18 biggest cities, had already run out.
"Our "svi, svi, svi (everybody)' action begins in four days," Draskovic said, referring to opposition plans to escalate their protests with a general blockade of traffic and public institutions.
Zajedno protests have halted traffic in the past, but nothing so ambitious has been attempted and the plans remained vague.
But with daily protests now well into their ninth week, crowds seem to be dwindling and opposition leaders appeared to be looking for fresh ways to increase pressure on Milosevic.
All three Zajedno leaders were due to fly to Rome later on Thursday for talks with Prime Minister Romano Prodi and Foreign Minister Lamberto Dini.

Zajedno also got a boost when Europe's biggest security body, the 54-nation Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE) based in Vienna, urged Milosevic to abandon "step-by-step concessions" and give seats to the opposition.
In addition, the European Parliament urged member states to freeze relations with Serbia until democracy had been established there.

But Zajedno continued to face an uphill contest in its battle of wills with the wily Milosevic and his entrenched Socialist party, whose hardline faction has showed no sign of willingness to cede the municipal councils.
An electoral commission said earlier this week that Zajedno had won in Belgrade and Serbia's second biggest city, Nis, but SPS hardliners say they will challenge the ruling.
"Our suspicion that the Socialists have no intention of giving up Belgrade is growing stronger and stronger," Zajedno co-leader Zoran Djindjic said.
"We expect the SPS to annul in the next two or three days the municipal electoral commission's decision, at the instructions of its president," he said.
"We cannot harbour any illusions. The hardliners are now the dominant faction in the SPS."
The Zajedno leaders responded to reports circulating in the Belgrade press that Milosevic had invited Draskovic and Djindjic to meet with him.

"Never in these past six years has our president called us to talk to him," Djindjic said. "In every normal country party leaders meet and discuss important matters when the future of the country is at stake, but this is not a normal country."
